title: Handing over the keys to the .'most haunted house in Stratford
excerpt: The famous ghosts of the most haunted house in Stratford are having to get used to new housemates.
content:
The famous ghosts of the most haunted house in Stratford are having to get used to new housemates.

The Shrieve’s House at 40 Sheep Street is 16th century, although a dwelling has stood on this spot since 1196.

It is more commonly known as being home to living history museum Tudor World, which welcomes visitors from all over the globe as well as hosting education visits from schools.

Lovingly run by Janet and John Ford for the last two decades, the popular couple decided to retire and last month gave over the running of the landmark to fresh hands.

The transition has been as seamless as a bed-sheet ghost costume, with Tudor World remaining open as Ben and Lisa Pugh have taken the reins.

Speaking about the decision to step down, John tells the Herald: “I’m 69 this year, and we’d been thinking about retiring for a while.

“Running the business has been demanding – we could never take any time off. After all the hassle of keeping things going during Covid and the sad deaths of some of our people, we felt that it was the right time to pass on the business.”

The couple have suffered the tragic loss of three friends and staff members in recent years. They include Penny Burton-Hind in 2021; and Shakespeare impersonators Ellis Creez and Kingsley Glover. Ellis died unexpectedly at the age of 43 in 2021; the loss of Kingsley followed just six months later, after he passed away from a heart condition at 39.

“Janet also lost her mum and brother,” continues John. “And with the sad deaths of our friends and colleagues that were so young, it’s given us pause for thought. We needed to take a break, and as much as we loved it, we were there for 18 years.”

Back in 2007, it was Janet’s idea to leave their original vocations and run their own business. She had been a teacher and John was a manager for Transport for London.

Janet spotted an advertisement to take over what was then known as the Falstaff Experience in a trade magazine. And so they came up from the south to run the historic property – which is leased from the Stratford Town Trust.

Now looking forward to retirement, the Fords, who live in Evesham, are planning a much-deserved holiday – a cruise around Norway’s fjords that will also serve to celebrate their 40th wedding anniversary.

“It’s hard to let it go in one way, but it’s also come as a bit of a relief and I feel a lot more relaxed now,” says John, who says he will miss “chatting to people” the most.

Reflecting on how they grew the business, John says making the experience a more curriculum-friendly and educational one was pivotal to its success: “When we took over we rebranded it Tudor World, and developed a good educational programme. We regularly entertained 500 schoolchildren a week, alongside family and tourist visits.

“The Shakespeare-led walking tour and ghost tours also became really popular,” adds John.

Ah, yes, ghosts. As well as having the highest phantom population in the district, Tudor World has been christened the UK’s ‘most haunted house’ by paranormal investigation groups who have been frequent visitors over the years.

In one memorable incident, famous medium Derek Acorah became possessed by a dark evil spirit while filming an episode of the TV programme Most Haunted at the venue in 2004.

Describing what happened in a letter to his sister, Derek – who died in 2020 – said: “From the moment I entered the building, I felt an overwhelming sense of anguish and dread, with many, many souls present in the atmosphere. There was certainly evidence of sorcery and witchcraft present everywhere with an almighty stench of rotting flesh all around me.

“As I made my way upstairs, I was aware of a particular bad soul, trying desperately to unnerve me. A gruesome experience of consummation and torture surrounded my whole body, leading me to the point of collapse. Fortunately, due to the quick thinking and response of my production crew, I was helped out of the building and to safety.”

The first known tenant of the building was William Shrieve, who was an archer to King Henry VIII, and he’s rumoured to still haunt his old home.

In the 16th century it was a tavern run by William Rogers who is said to have been the inspiration for Shakespeare’s famous comic character Sir John Falstaff. And while the rotund bon vivant may not be among the house’s haunters, his spirit lives on in the town’s public houses.

“Quite a few of the paranormal people, including Acorah, picked up on a malevolent spirit known as John Davis,” says John, as he recounts the house’s notorious ghoulies. “He is said to intimidate women and has bad breath.”

“Another sighting is of little urchin girl, Lucy – they say she was a pickpocket. Quite a few female visitors have said they have felt her tug on their clothes. And I felt a small hand take my fingers as I was sleeping – when my arm was hanging off the bed.

“One encounter I had was a couple of weeks after we’d first taken it over. I was in the museum area and I looked through a door and saw a hooded figure with red eyes.

“I’ve also been tapped on the shoulder with no-one around.”

A visitor from the animal spirit world also sticks in John’s mind.

“I was in bed and felt a cat padding its paws on me – there was no cat when I opened my eyes but the weird thing was there was an indent where something had been sitting.”

Janet and John are relieved that the business is continuing to thrive in the safe hands of Ben and Lisa.

The couple moved into Shrieve’s House in the summer with daughters Erin, 10, and Erin, 13.

Ben had worked with John and Janet at Tudor World previously, and had been particularly involved on the creative programming side. He has also worked at Warwick Castle where he gained skills in historical interpretation

“I’ve always liked performing arts,” he tells the Herald. “And when John and Janet said the business was available, we couldn’t resist the opportunity to write our family history into the Shrieve’s House and into the history of the Tudor World, it is such a truly magical and unique place.”

He continues: “Erin is enjoying putting on Tudor outfits and helping in the shop. Jess is mad about football, but we all share a passion for history.”

Sharing their approach to managing the attraction, Ben says: “If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it. I believe very fully in what John and Janet have built here. We’ll be adding small things – like there’s a new feature of a captain’s chest which will allow visitors to play with compasses and create their own maps.”

The Pughs are keen to get to know business neighbours and residents in the town: “Building close relationships in the local community is important to us, and hearing the input of others. We’ll be keeping our prices low too. As a family, we understand how difficult managing finances can be at the moment, so we’re not messing with our price. We want to be affordable and accessible. We want to share this building with everybody.”

And that would appear to be the ghosts too – with daughter Erin having already encountered friendly child ghost ‘Lucy’.
